newsitem.title: CONGO: Grinning Kabila, grim Mobutu meet at Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Grinning Kabila, grim Mobutu meet at Zaire talks.

text.p: When they finally appeared together in public, the chief protagonists in Zaire's civil war could not have painted a more contrasting picture.
Ailing and embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko sat frail and grim-faced at a news conference wrapping up his historic meeting with guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila aboard a South African navy ship.
Kabila had entered the press room in SAS Outeniqua's forecastle quarters smiling and brimming with confidence.
South African President Nelson Mandela, who is mediating in Zaire's seven-month-old conflict, sat between the two men.
Neither Mobutu nor Kabila made any attempt to look in the other's direction. Mobutu leaned forward, listening intently as Mandela spoke to reporters at the brief news conference.
The first direct talks between the two Zairean arch-rivals finally took place on Sunday on the Outeniqua in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.
"The face-to-face meeting was very African. There was communication," said U.N. special envoy on the Zaire crisis, Mohamed Sahnoun, who partcipated in the talks.

"Perhaps at he start it's normal there was tension on each side. Then there was a cordial turn -- very African. There were no poisonous remarks," he told reporters on the ship in the first eyewitness account of the high-security meeting.
But even such diplomatic language could not mask Mobutu's humiliation in the farcical drama leading up to the talks.
Reporters were kept far away from the conference chamber, in the form of two windowless containers joined together on the Outeniqua's deck.
Neither Kabila nor Mobutu spoke at the news conference at which Sahnoun read a communique announcing that Mandela would convene another round of talks in about a week.

It reiterated Kabila's uncompromising call for the resignation of Mobutu and handover of power to his guerrilla alliance as a condition for a ceasefire. Mobutu maintained his demand for a transition process leading to elections.
Reporters were specifically ordered not to direct questions to the two rivals and Mandela took only two questions.

Mandela had convened the meeting with U.S. and United Nations backing in a desperate attempt to prevent Kabila's rebels attacking the Zairean capital Kinshasa after seizing control of most of the vast country's territory.

The talks had been dogged by problems as both men argued over a venue. Last-minute U.S. diplomacy prevailed on the two to agree to meet aboard the customised icebreaker last Friday, amid complex security arrangements.

But in a humuliating snub to Mobutu, Kabila, citing security worries, refused to travel to the ship, keeping the cancer-stricken Mobutu waiting in Pointe Noire for two days. Mandela spent two nights on the ship as negotiators tried to salvage the meeting.
Kabila's forces have seized most major towns in Zaire and say they are close to taking Kinshasa.
